note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Maintain quality systems within a team

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a quality management system in a fabrication shop?
options: To add extra paperwork to each job so that every job takes longer to finish
So work is planned, done and checked the same way, to meet requirements
To give the manager a way to find someone to blame for each fault
To let the shop charge customers more for the same work as before

questions.stem: Which list shows the usual levels of quality documents, from the top down?
options: Forms, records, work instructions, procedures, manual, policy
Procedures, policy, records, manual, forms, work instructions
Records, manual, policy, forms, work instructions, procedures
Policy, manual, procedures, work instructions, forms and records

questions.stem: What is a quality policy?
options: Management's short statement of commitment to quality
A detailed list of every check made on every weld in the shop
An insurance policy that pays out when a customer complains
A list of the prices charged for each kind of repair job

questions.stem: Which is a well-written quality objective for a welding team?
options: Try to make the welds better and neater from now on
Do quality work at all times and keep the customer happy
Cut weld repairs from 6% to 3% of joints by the end of March
Have fewer problems with welds than the other teams this year

questions.stem: In a quality system, what is a team leader's main quality job?
options: To carry out every inspection personally, so that nobody else needs to
To see the team knows and follows procedures, and records are kept
To write the company's quality policy and sign it each year
To deal with all customer complaints without telling the manager

questions.stem: A welder finds a photocopy of a procedure, with no revision mark, taped to a booth wall. What should the team leader do?
options: Leave it, since any copy of a procedure is better than none at all
Write today's date on it so that it becomes the current version
Ask the welders to vote on whether the copy is still correct
Remove it, check the current version, and put up a controlled copy

questions.stem: Who should approve a change to a work instruction?
options: The person given that authority in the system
Any welder who finds a faster way to do the job
The customer, every time any change is made
Nobody, since work instructions never change

questions.stem: What is the difference between a document and a record in a quality system?
options: A document is on paper, and a record is always on a computer
A document is for customers, and a record is only for managers
A document says what to do; a record shows what was done
There is no difference; the two words mean the same thing

questions.stem: How long should quality records, such as weld inspection sheets, be kept?
options: Until the end of the week the job was finished
For the time set in the system or the contract
Only until the customer has paid the invoice
For as long as there is room in the office

questions.stem: Which is the right way to keep electronic inspection records secure?
options: On each inspector's own phone, so they are always to hand
On a shared computer with no password, so anyone can update them
On one memory stick that is kept in the team leader's drawer
In the agreed system, with access controls and backups

questions.stem: Why does a quality system keep a register of all measuring and test equipment?
options: So that each item can be tracked and none is used after its calibration is due
So that the equipment can be insured for its full value every year
So that nobody else is allowed to borrow any of the tools
So that the equipment can be sold when the next model comes out

questions.stem: A calibration check finds a digital caliper reading 0.3 mm out. Apart from taking it out of use, what else must the team leader do?
options: Nothing else, since 0.3 mm is far too small to matter on any job
Adjust all the drawings by 0.3 mm to match the caliper's readings
Check the work measured with it since its last good check
Give the caliper to a trainee for practice on scrap only

questions.stem: Why is a welding machine's current display checked against a calibrated meter?
options: To find out how much electricity the machine uses each month
So the current recorded truly matches the WPS limits
To prove the machine is new enough to be under guarantee
So the machine can be run at a higher current than its rating

questions.stem: What is the difference between a hold point and a witness point in an inspection plan?
options: A hold point is only for welds, and a witness point is only for painting work
A hold point is held by the client; a witness point is held by the welder
They are the same thing, and the two names can be swapped freely
Work stops at a hold point until released; at a witness point it may go on

questions.stem: Why should the person who gives final acceptance to a weld usually not be the person who made it?
options: An independent check is less likely to miss faults
Welders are not trained to look at any welds at all
The welder will always hide their own faults on purpose
Final inspection is always done by the customer

questions.stem: A procedure says to check 1 in every 10 brackets. In a batch of 120, 2 of the 12 checked are faulty. What should the team leader do?
options: Accept the batch, since only 2 of the brackets were found faulty
Throw away the 2 faulty brackets and send the rest to the customer
Stop, keep the batch apart, and check more or all of them
Check the next batch more closely, but send this batch out

questions.stem: A non-conforming part has been found. What is meant by its 'disposition'?
options: The name of the welder who made the faulty part
The decision on what to do with it: rework, repair, accept or scrap
The place in the workshop where the fault was first seen by someone
The cost of the part as shown on the customer's invoice

questions.stem: When can a non-conforming part be used 'as is', without repair?
options: Whenever the job is running late and the team is in a hurry
Whenever the welder who made it says it is good enough to use
Whenever the fault cannot easily be seen once it is painted
Only when the customer or an authorised person agrees in writing

questions.stem: What is the difference between corrective action and preventive action?
options: Corrective fixes the cause of a problem that happened; preventive, one that could
Corrective action is done by managers, and preventive action is done by welders
Corrective action costs money; preventive action is always free to do
There is no difference; both words mean fixing the faulty part itself

questions.stem: A corrective action was put in place a month ago. How does the team leader check that it worked?
options: Ask the person who suggested it whether they think it worked
Assume it worked, since nobody in the team has complained about it yet
Look at the records since then to see if the problem has come back
Wait for the next audit, which will happen in about a year

questions.stem: What is an internal quality audit?
options: A surprise check of the workers' bags at the end of each working day
A planned check that the team follows its system and that it works
A count of all the money taken in by the business each month
A test of each welder's skill on a new test piece

questions.stem: An auditor asks to see last week's electrode oven log. It has gaps. What should the team leader do?
options: Fill in the gaps quickly from memory before handing the log over
Say that the log was lost and that it will be found later
Blame the store keeper and say it is nothing to do with the team
Be honest, accept the finding, and agree a corrective action

questions.stem: Why should an auditor not audit their own work area?
options: To keep the audit fair and independent
Because they would find too many faults in it
Because it would take them far too long to do
Because auditors are not allowed in workshops

questions.stem: What is 'objective evidence' in an audit?
options: What the team leader says usually happens in the workshop
The auditor's own feeling about how tidy the area looks
Facts that can be checked, such as records and measurements
The answers given by whoever is nearest to the auditor

questions.stem: Why does a quality system keep training records for each team member?
options: To decide who gets the most overtime each month
To show each person is competent for their tasks
To work out each person's holiday entitlement
So that the records can be sent to the customer

questions.stem: A new procedure for controlling low-hydrogen electrodes is issued. How should the team leader roll it out?
options: Pin it on the notice board and expect everyone to read it in their own time
Tell the most senior welder and let him pass it on to the others
Wait until a problem happens, then explain the new procedure
Brief the team, show the method, check understanding, record the training

questions.stem: In the PDCA cycle, what happens at the 'Act' stage?
options: The change is made standard if it worked, or tried again if not
The first plan is written down and approved by the manager
The new idea is tried out for the first time on a small job
The results are measured and compared with the plan

questions.stem: What is a check sheet (tally sheet) used for in quality work?
options: Checking the time each worker arrives in the morning
Listing the tools that must be returned to the store
Counting how often each type of fault happens
Writing the cheque to pay a supplier's invoice

questions.stem: A Pareto chart of weld repairs shows porosity causes 55% and undercut 20%. Where should the team put its effort first?
options: On undercut
On porosity
Equally on all faults
On the smallest causes

questions.stem: What is a control chart used for?
options: To show who in the team is in control of each job
To list the controls on each welding machine
To show the layout of the controls in the store
To see if a process stays steady or starts to drift

questions.stem: Why are steel and consumable suppliers checked and listed in a quality system?
options: So materials come from sources known to give the right quality
So the cheapest supplier is always used, whatever the quality of the goods
So that only one supplier is ever used for every item
So the suppliers can inspect the shop's finished work

questions.stem: A delivery of E7018 electrodes arrives with damaged, open tins. What should the team leader do?
options: Put them in the oven straight away and use them on the next job
Use the damaged tins first so that they do not go to waste
Keep them apart, record it, and tell the supplier and the store
Throw them away at once without telling anyone about it

questions.stem: A crack is found in a weld on a hotel balcony two months after handover. What makes it possible to find the welder, consumables and inspection involved?
options: The memory of the team members who worked on the balcony
Records such as the weld map and batch numbers
The customer's own notes about the work being done
The supplier's invoice for the steel that was used

questions.stem: Why is customer feedback part of a quality system?
options: So the business can decide which customers to stop serving
So that every customer can be offered a discount on the next job
So the team leader can find out which customers complain the most
It shows if work meets customers' needs, and where to improve

questions.stem: A customer complaint comes in. What should the quality system make sure happens?
options: It is logged, investigated, answered and used to improve
It is passed to the welder who did the job to sort out alone
It is kept quiet so that the business's name is not harmed
It is answered only if the customer complains a second time

questions.stem: A welder says the inspection checklist takes too long and wants to skip it on small jobs. What should the team leader do?
options: Agree, since small jobs never have any faults that are worth checking
Tell him that he will lose his job if he says it again
Explain why it matters, and propose any better way through the system
Let him skip it on Fridays when the team is busiest

questions.stem: How does a team leader build a 'quality culture' in the team?
options: By punishing every mistake in front of the whole team
By doing all the important welds personally so they are right
By keeping the quality results secret from the team
By talking openly about faults, finding the cause and agreeing how to prevent them

questions.stem: A team member hides a faulty weld instead of reporting it, because he fears blame. What does this tell the team leader?
options: That the team member should be moved to another team at once
That the quality checklist needs to be made much longer
That faulty welds are not important enough to report
The team needs to feel safe to report faults without blame

questions.stem: Why does the team review its quality results at a regular meeting?
options: To spot trends early and agree actions
To decide who will be paid a bonus
To fill time when there is no work
To prepare a list of people to blame

questions.stem: A team welded 400 joints this month and 14 needed repair. What is the repair rate?
Rework cost J$120 000 last quarter. A new electrode oven costs J$90 000 and is expected to halve the rework. About how many quarters until the saving pays for the oven?
options: 3 quarters
1.5 quarters
0.75 quarters
2 quarters

questions.stem: A team's pass rate at inspection rose from 88% to 94%. By how many percentage points did it rise?
A customer asks whether the Centre's quality system is certified to an international quality standard. What does certification mean?
options: The Centre has bought a copy of the standard and keeps it in the office
The team leader has signed a letter saying the system is good
Outside auditors checked it and found it meets the standard
The customer has visited and liked what they saw in the shop

questions.stem: A team leader wants to try a new way of tacking frames. What is the best way under a quality system?
options: Change the method on all jobs at once, without telling anyone else about it
Trial it, measure the results, then update the procedure if it works
Wait until the customer asks for the method to be changed
Ask each welder to choose the method they like best

questions.stem: What happens at a management review of the quality system?
options: The managers check each welder's work one weld at a time in every bay
The managers decide the prices for next year's jobs
The managers interview each customer about the staff
Senior staff review audits, complaints and objectives, and plan improvements

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters ITP stand for: the plan that lists each inspection and test on a job?
What is the name for the written agreement from the customer that lets a non-conforming item be used as it is?
What is the name for keeping faulty or doubtful items apart in a marked area until a decision is made?
A team checks 1 in every 8 items. How many items are checked in a batch of 96?
What is the name for an audit finding where a requirement is not being met?
What is the name of the cause-and-effect diagram shaped like the skeleton of a fish?
In the quality term QA, the Q stands for 'quality'. What does the A stand for?
What is the name of the independent organisation that audits a business's quality system and issues a certificate?
In a batch of 250 parts, 5 were rejected. What percentage passed?
A gauge is calibrated every 6 months. It was last calibrated on 15 May 2026. In which month is it next due?
What is the name of the log in which every customer complaint is recorded?
How many percentage points apart are a 92% pass rate and a 97% pass rate?
Give the number of the best-known international standard for quality management systems (ISO ....).
What is the name of the record that shows a measuring tool was checked against a standard, with the date and the results?
What is the name for a welder checking their own work before handing it on?

essays.stem: Describe the main parts of a quality management system in a welding and fabrication business, and explain the team leader's role in keeping it working day to day.
essays.modelAnswer: A quality management system has a quality policy and objectives set by management; a manual that describes the system; procedures that say how key tasks are done, such as receiving materials, welding to a WPS, inspection and dealing with faults; work instructions and forms for each task; and records that prove what was done, such as inspection sheets, calibration records and training records. It also includes audits, corrective actions, customer feedback and management review. The team leader keeps it working day to day by making sure the team has the current documents, knows the procedures and follows them; that measuring tools are in calibration; that inspections and records are done properly and on time; that faults are reported, kept apart and recorded; and that problems and ideas are passed on for improvement. The team leader also trains new members, leads by example, and takes part in audits honestly.
markingPoints: Policy, objectives and manual
Procedures, work instructions, forms and records
Audits, corrective action, customer feedback and review
Team leader ensures current documents, procedures followed, calibration, records
Team leader handles faults, training, improvement ideas and audits

essays.stem: Explain how document control works for procedures, drawings and WPSs, and what the team leader does when a document is changed.
essays.modelAnswer: Each controlled document has a number, a title, a revision letter or number, a date, and an approval signature. A master list shows the current revision of every document and where copies are kept. Changes are requested, reviewed and approved by an authorised person before they are issued, and the reason for the change is recorded. When a new revision is issued, the old copies are collected and destroyed or marked 'superseded', and one master copy of the old version is kept for the record. Uncontrolled copies, such as photocopies, are marked so that nobody works from them. When a document changes, the team leader collects the old copies from the workshop, puts the new ones in place, tells the team what has changed and why, checks they understand, and records that they were briefed. Work already in progress is checked to see if it is affected.
markingPoints: Number, title, revision, date and approval on each document
Master list of current revisions and copy holders
Changes reviewed and approved; reason recorded
Old copies withdrawn or marked superseded; uncontrolled copies marked
Team leader replaces copies, briefs the team, records it, checks work in progress

essays.stem: A batch of 60 welded brackets is found to have undersized fillet welds after 40 have been painted. Explain how you would handle the non-conformance from finding it to closing it out.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would stop work on the brackets and tag the whole batch, painted and unpainted, keeping them apart so none are sent out. I would raise a non-conformance report giving the job, drawing and revision, the required weld size, the sizes measured, how many are affected, and photos. I would check every bracket, not just a sample. Then the supervisor, and the customer if needed, decide the disposition: for example, strip the paint and add weld to bring them to size under an approved repair method, or scrap them. The repaired brackets are inspected again and repainted. Next I would find the root cause: perhaps the welder had an old drawing, the gauge was not used, or inspection was skipped before painting. A corrective action is agreed, such as making weld inspection a hold point before painting, with an owner and a date. When the brackets pass and the action has been checked, the NCR is signed off and filed.
markingPoints: Stops work, tags and keeps the whole batch apart
Raises an NCR with full details and checks every bracket
Disposition decided by the right people; repair, re-inspection and repainting
Finds the root cause and agrees a corrective action with owner and date
Checks the action worked; signs off and files the NCR

essays.stem: Explain how to prepare for and take part in an internal quality audit of your team's work area, and how to respond to the findings.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the audit I would read the audit plan to see which procedures will be checked, such as electrode control and weld inspection. I would make sure the current documents are in place, the records are complete and filed, the measuring tools have current calibration labels, and the area is tidy. I would brief the team that the audit is to check the system, not to blame people, and that they should answer honestly and show what they do. During the audit I would go with the auditor, answer questions truthfully, show records when asked, and not hide problems. If something is missing, I would say so. After the audit, I would read the findings, agree with the auditor what each one means, and find the cause of each non-conformity. Then I would agree corrective actions with an owner and a date, carry them out, and give the auditor evidence that they were done and worked.
markingPoints: Reads the audit plan; checks documents, records, calibration, housekeeping
Briefs the team that the audit checks the system and to be honest
During the audit: accompanies, answers truthfully, shows records
After: understands findings and finds causes
Agrees and completes corrective actions with owner, date and evidence

essays.stem: Explain how the calibration of measuring and test equipment is controlled in a quality system, and what you would do if an item is found out of calibration.
essays.modelAnswer: Every measuring and test item, such as tapes, calipers, weld gauges, thermometers and machine meters, is given an ID number and listed on a register with its calibration interval and due date. Each is checked against a known standard, by the Centre's competent person or an outside laboratory, and a calibration certificate is kept. A label on the item shows its ID and due date. Items are stored and handled carefully, and users check them before use, for example zeroing a caliper. Items that are overdue are taken out of use. If an item is found out of calibration, I would take it out of use and label it, record the error found, and then check all the work measured with it since its last good calibration, to see whether any of that work could be wrong. If so, the work is re-measured and an NCR raised for anything that fails. The item is repaired, adjusted and recalibrated, or scrapped.
markingPoints: ID number and register with interval and due date
Calibrated against a known standard; certificate kept; label on the item
Careful storage and checks before use; overdue items withdrawn
Out of calibration: withdraw, label, record the error
Checks work measured since the last good calibration; NCR if needed; repair or scrap

essays.stem: Describe how you would use quality data (check sheets, Pareto charts and repair rates) to find and reduce the most common weld faults in your team.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would set up a check sheet at the inspection point, with a column for each type of fault, such as porosity, undercut, lack of fusion and wrong size, and ask the inspectors to tally every fault they find, with the date, job and welder. After a month I would add up the totals and draw a Pareto chart, with the faults in order from most to least. This usually shows that one or two faults cause most of the repairs. I would also work out the repair rate, such as repairs ÷ joints welded × 100, each week. For the biggest fault, say porosity, I would hold a short meeting with the team to find the causes, using a fishbone diagram, and agree actions such as checking the electrode oven and screening draughts. I would keep collecting data to see whether the repair rate falls, and then move on to the next biggest fault.
markingPoints: Check sheet tallying each fault type with date, job and welder
Pareto chart to find the biggest faults
Repair rate worked out and tracked
Team finds causes (for example fishbone) and agrees actions
Keeps measuring to see if it worked, then moves to the next fault

essays.stem: Explain how you would train and involve your team so that they own quality, including how you would deal with someone who does not follow procedures.
essays.modelAnswer: I would make sure every member is trained in the procedures for their work, such as the WPS, inspection checklists and how to report faults, and record that training. I would explain why each check matters, using real examples of what goes wrong, so it is not just paperwork. The team would be involved in setting quality targets, reviewing results at regular meetings, and suggesting improvements, and I would act on good ideas and give credit. I would praise good work and treat faults as a chance to learn, so that people report problems rather than hide them. If someone does not follow a procedure, I would first talk to them privately to find out why: they may not understand it, may lack time or tools, or the procedure may be unworkable. I would retrain or fix the problem, and make clear what is expected. If it carries on, I would follow the Centre's disciplinary procedure and record what happened.
markingPoints: Trains everyone in the procedures and records it
Explains why checks matter with real examples
Involves the team in targets, reviews and improvements; gives credit
Blame-free reporting; praises good work
Deals with non-compliance privately, finds the cause, retrains; follows Centre procedure if it continues

essays.stem: Describe how traceability is kept on a structural steel job, from receiving the materials to handover, and why it matters.
essays.modelAnswer: When steel arrives, it is checked against the order and its mill certificate, and the heat (cast) number is recorded and kept marked on each piece, including offcuts that will be used. Consumables such as electrodes and wire have their batch numbers recorded, with their certificates. Each weld is numbered on a weld map, and the records link each weld to the WPS used, the welder's ID, the consumable batch, the date, and the inspection and test results. Repairs and NCRs are linked to the same weld numbers. At handover, the customer gets a data book with the certificates, weld map, inspection records and as-built drawings, and the Centre keeps a copy for the agreed time. Traceability matters because if a fault or failure is found later, the cause can be traced to a material batch, a welder or a procedure, and other parts that may have the same problem can be found quickly.
markingPoints: Materials checked against mill certificates; heat numbers recorded and kept on pieces
Consumable batch numbers and certificates recorded
Weld map links each weld to WPS, welder, batch, date and inspection
Handover data book; copies kept
Explains why: trace causes and find other affected parts

essays.stem: Explain how customer complaints and feedback should be handled in a quality system, using a complaint about a gate that is rusting a month after it was fitted as an example.
essays.modelAnswer: The complaint is logged in the complaints register with the customer's details, the job number and a description, and the customer is thanked and told when they will hear back. Someone is given the task of investigating. In the rusting gate example, I would visit, take photos and check the records: the paint system specified, the surface preparation, the paint batch, the conditions when it was painted, and whether the welds were cleaned before painting. Suppose the records show the welds were painted over flux and spatter without proper cleaning. The gate would be repaired by cleaning back and repainting, at no cost to the customer, and the customer told what was found and done. The root cause leads to a corrective action, such as adding a surface-preparation check as a hold point before painting. The complaint is closed when the customer is satisfied, and complaints are reviewed regularly to find trends.
markingPoints: Logs the complaint and replies to the customer promptly
Investigates with a visit, photos and records
Puts the problem right and tells the customer what was found
Finds the root cause and takes corrective action
Closes it when the customer is satisfied and reviews trends

essays.stem: Describe the PDCA cycle and show how you would use it to make and test one improvement in your team's work.
essays.modelAnswer: PDCA stands for Plan, Do, Check, Act. In Plan, the problem is defined with data, the cause is found, and a change is planned with a target. In Do, the change is tried, often on a small scale. In Check, the results are measured and compared with the target. In Act, if it worked the change is made standard, for example by updating the procedure and training the team; if not, the team learns from it and goes round the cycle again. Example: the team's records show that 8% of frames are out of square after welding. Plan: we find that frames are tacked without a check of the diagonals, and plan to add a diagonal check after tacking, with a target of under 3%. Do: we try it on the next 20 frames. Check: only one frame is out of square (5%), better but not on target. Act: we keep the check and add clamping to a jig, then run the cycle again.
markingPoints: Explains Plan: define the problem, find the cause, plan a change with a target
Explains Do: try the change on a small scale
Explains Check: measure and compare with the target
Explains Act: make it standard or repeat the cycle
Gives a clear workshop example taken through all four stages

practical1.title: Carry out an internal audit of a workshop area against a procedure, and plan corrective actions
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a short written procedure used at the Centre (for example, the control of welding electrodes: storage, oven use, issue and return, and the oven log) and sets up the area to be audited, with some things done right and some not. As a group, plan the audit: write an audit checklist from the procedure and agree who checks which part. Carry out the audit by looking at the area, the records (oven log, issue sheets, calibration label on the oven thermometer) and by asking the 'store keeper' (played by the assessor) questions. Record the objective evidence for each point: what was seen, the record, the date. Then write up the findings, each marked as conforming or non-conforming, with the evidence. For each non-conformity, find the likely cause and write a corrective action with an owner and a date. Finish with a 5-minute closing meeting with the assessor. Each member leads at least one part of the checklist. Photograph each stage and add the photos, checklist and findings to the group's practical.
materials: The procedure to audit (from the assessor)
The audit area set up by the assessor, with its records (oven log, issue sheets, labels)
Audit checklist and findings templates, or a computer with a word processor
Clipboards, pens and a camera or phone
photos: Members checking the area against the checklist
A record being checked (for example the oven log)
Evidence of a non-conformity, photographed with a label
The corrective action plan with owners and dates
The closing meeting with the assessor
checklist: Helped write a checklist that covers the procedure
Led their part of the audit and recorded objective evidence
Graded each finding correctly as conforming or non-conforming
Found a sensible cause for each non-conformity
Wrote corrective actions that are specific, with an owner and a date
Took part in the closing meeting and explained findings without blame
safety: Do not touch the hot electrode oven; read its display only
Wear safety glasses and boots in the workshop area
Do not move or open gas cylinders or machines during the audit
Keep personal details in records confidential

practical2.title: Run quality control on a batch of welded parts: inspect, record, analyse and raise a non-conformance
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a batch of 20–30 welded parts (for example fillet-welded brackets) made to a drawing, with some faults built in, and the measuring tools to use. First, as a group, check that each gauge and measuring tool is in calibration and zeroed, and record this. Each member then inspects a share of the parts against the drawing and an inspection checklist (size, leg length, squareness, visible weld faults) and records the results on a check sheet. The group adds up the faults, makes a Pareto chart, and works out the reject rate. For the faulty parts, the group tags them and keeps them apart, raises a non-conformance report with evidence and a proposed disposition, finds the most likely root cause using the five whys or a fishbone diagram, and proposes a corrective action with an owner and a date. Finally, the group presents its results to the assessor, who acts as the supervisor. Photograph each stage and add the photos and records to the group's practical.
materials: A batch of 20–30 welded parts with built-in faults, and their drawing
Fillet weld gauges, a steel rule, a square, a tape and a caliper, with calibration labels
Inspection checklist, check sheet, NCR form and graph paper or a spreadsheet
Reject tags or labels, and a marked quarantine area or box
photos: The gauges and tools with their calibration labels, and the record of checks
A member measuring a weld with a fillet gauge
The Pareto chart and the reject rate calculation
The faulty parts tagged and kept apart
The root cause diagram and the corrective action
checklist: Checked tools were in calibration and zeroed before use
